entries.title: Job 36:1
segments:
. 
 
    1, 2. Elihu maintains that afflictions are to the godly disciplinary, in order to lead them to attain a higher moral worth, and that the reason for their continuance is not, as the friends asserted, on account of the sufferer's extraordinary guilt, but because the discipline has not yet attained its object, namely, to lend him to humble himself penitently before God (
). This is Elihu's fourth speech. He thus exceeds the ternary number of the others. Hence his formula of politeness (
). Literally, "Wait yet but a little for me." Bear with me a little farther. I have yet (much,
). There are Chaldeisms in this verse, agreeably to the view that the scene of the book is near the Euphrates and the Chaldees.

entries.title: Job 36:3
segments:
3. from afar--not trite commonplaces, but drawn from God's mighty works. 
 
    ascribe righteousness--whereas Job ascribed unrighteousness (

). A man, in enquiring into God's ways, should at the outset presume they are all just, be willing to find them so, and expect that the result of investigation will prove them to be so; such a one will never be disappointed [BARNES].

entries.title: Job 36:4
segments: 4. I will not "speak wickedly for God," as the friends (

) --that is, vindicate God by unsound arguments. 
 
    he that is perfect, &c.--Rather, as the parallelism requires, "a man of integrity in sentiments is with thee" (is he with whom thou hast to do). Elihu means himself, as opposed to the dishonest reasonings of the friends (

entries.title: Job 36:5
segments: 5. Rather, "strength of understanding" (heart) the force of the repetition of "mighty"; as "mighty" as God is, none is too low to be "despised" by Him; for His "might" lies especially in "His strength of understanding," whereby He searches out the most minute things, so as to give to each his right. Elihu confirms his exhortation (

entries.title: Job 36:6
segments: 6. right ... poor--He espouses the cause of the afflicted.

entries.title: Job 36:7
segments: ). God does not forsake the godly, as Job implied, but "establishes," or makes them sit on the throne as kings (
). True of believers in the highest sense, already in part (
); hereafter fully (

). 
 
    and they are--that they may be.

entries.title: Job 36:8
segments: 8-10. If they be afflicted, it is no proof that they are hypocrites, as the friends maintain, or that God disregards them, and is indifferent whether men are good or bad, as Job asserts: God is thereby "disciplining them," and "showing them their sins," and if they bow in a right spirit under God's visiting hand, the greatest blessings ensue.

entries.title: Job 36:9
segments:
9. work--transgression. 
 
    that ... exceeded--"In that they behaved themselves mightily" (literally, "great"); that is, presumptuously, or, at least, self-confidently.

entries.title: Job 36:11
segments: 11. serve--that is, worship; as in
. God is to be supplied (compare

segments:

    without knowledge--that is, on account of their foolishness (

entries.title: Job 36:13
segments: 13-15. Same sentiment as

, expanded. 
 
    hypocrites--or, the ungodly [MAURER]; but "hypocrites" is perhaps a distinct class from the openly wicked (

). 
 
    heap up wrath--of God against themselves (

). UMBREIT translates, "nourish their wrath against God," instead of "crying" unto Him. This suits well the parallelism and the Hebrew. But the English Version gives a good parallelism, "hypocrites" answering to "cry not" (
); "heap up wrath" against themselves, to "He bindeth them" with fetters of affliction (

entries.title: Job 36:14
segments: 14. Rather (

), Their life is (ended) as that of (literally, "among") the unclean, prematurely and dishonorably. So the second clause answers to the first. A warning that Job make not common cause with the wicked (

entries.title: Job 36:15
segments:
15. poor--the afflicted pious. 
 
    openeth ... ears-- (
); so as to be admonished in their straits ("oppression") to seek God penitently, and so be "delivered" (

entries.title: Job 36:16
segments: 16. Rather, "He will lead forth thee also out of the jaws of a strait" (

). 
 
    broad place--expresses the liberty, and the well-supplied "table" the abundance of the prosperous (

entries.title: Job 36:17
segments: 17. Rather, "But if thou art fulfilled (that is, entirely filled) with the judgment of the wicked (that is, the guilt incurring judgment" [MAURER]; or rather, as UMBREIT, referring to
, the judgment pronounced on God by the guilty in misfortunes), judgment (God's judgment on the wicked,
, playing on the double meaning of "judgment") and justice shall closely follow each other [UMBREIT].

entries.title: Job 36:18
segments: ). Even the "ransom" by Jesus Christ (
) will be of no avail to wilful despisers (

). 
 
    with his stroke-- (
). UMBREIT translates, "Beware lest the wrath of God (thy severe calamity) lead thee to scorn" (

). This accords better with the verb in the parallel clause, which ought to be translated, "Let not the great ransom (of money, which thou canst give) seduce thee (Margin, turn thee aside, as if thou couldst deliver thyself from "wrath" by it). As the "scorn" in the first clause answers to the "judgment of the wicked" (
), so "ransom" ("seduce") to "will he esteem riches" (
). Thus,
is the transition between

entries.title: Job 36:19
segments: 19. forces of strength--that is, resources of wealth (

entries.title: Job 36:20
segments: 20. Desire--rant for. Job had wished for death (

, &c.). 
 
    night-- (

); so "cut off," "disappear." 
 
    in their place--literally, "under themselves"; so, without moving from their place, on the spot, suddenly (

) [MAURER].  UMBREIT'S translation: "To ascend (which is really, as thou wilt find to thy cost, to descend) to the people below" (literally, "under themselves"), answers better to the parallelism and the Hebrew. Thou pantest for death as desirable, but it is a "night" or region of darkness; thy fancied ascent (amelioration) will prove a descent (deterioration) (
); therefore desire it not.

entries.title: Job 36:21
segments:
21. regard--literally, "turn thyself to." 
 
    iniquity--namely, presumptuous speaking against God (
, and above, see on

    rather than--to bear "affliction" with pious patience. Men think it an alleviation to complain against God, but this is adding sin to sorrow; it is sin, not sorrow, which can really hurt us (contrast

entries.title: Job 36:22
segments:
22-25. God is not to be impiously arraigned, but to be praised for His might, shown in His works. 
 
    exalteth--rather, doeth lofty things, shows His exalted power [UMBREIT] (

). 
 
    teacheth-- (
, &c.). The connection is, returning to
, God's "might" is shown in His "wisdom"; He alone can teach; yet, because He, as a sovereign, explains not all His dealings, forsooth Job must presume to teach Him (
). So the transition to
is natural. UMBREIT with the Septuagint translates, "Who is Lord," wrongly, as this meaning belongs to later Hebrew.

entries.title: Job 36:23
segments: 23. Job dared to prescribe to God what He should do (

entries.title: Job 36:24
segments: 24. Instead of arraigning, let it be thy fixed principle to magnify God in His works (
); these, which all may "see," may convince us that what we do not see is altogether wise and good (

). 
 
    behold--As "see" (
), shows; not, as MAURER, "sing," laud (see on

entries.title: Job 36:25
segments:
25. See--namely, with wondering admiration [MAURER]. 
 
    man may behold--rather, "(yet) mortals (a different Hebrew word from 'man') behold it (only) from afar off," see but a small "part" (

entries.title: Job 36:26
segments:
). God's greatness in heaven and earth: a reason why Job should bow under His afflicting hand. 
 
    know him not--only in part (

). 
 
    his years-- (

entries.title: Job 36:27
segments: 27, 28. The marvellous formation of rain (so

). 
 
    maketh small--Rather, "He draweth (up) to Him, He attracts (from the earth below) the drops of water; they (the drops of water) pour down rain, (which is) His vapor." "Vapor" is in apposition with "rain," marking the way in which rain is formed; namely, from the vapor drawn up by God into the air and then condensed into drops, which fall (

). The suspension of such a mass of water, and its descent not in a deluge, but in drops of vapory rain, are the marvel. The selection of this particular illustration of God's greatness forms a fit prelude to the storm in which God appears (

entries.title: Job 36:28
segments: 28. abundantly--literally, "upon many men."

entries.title: Job 36:29
segments:
). God's marvels in thunder and lightnings. 
 
    spreadings, &c.--the canopy of thick clouds, which covers the heavens in a storm (

entries.title: Job 36:30
segments:
30. light--lightning. 
 
    it--His tabernacle (

). The light, in an instant spread over the vast mass of dark clouds, forms a striking picture. 
 
    spread--is repeated from

to form an antithesis. "He spreads not only clouds, but light." 
 
    covereth the bottom--roots. 
 
    of the sea--namely, with the light. In the storm the depths of ocean are laid bare; and the light "covers" them, at the same moment that it "spreads" across the dark sky. So in
, the discovering of "the channels of waters" follows the "lightnings." UMBREIT translates: "He spreadeth His light upon Himself, and covereth Himself with the roots of the sea" (

). God's garment is woven of celestial light and of the watery depths, raised to the sky to form His cloudy canopy. The phrase, "cover Himself with the roots of the sea," is harsh; but the image is grand.

entries.title: Job 36:31
segments: 31. These (rain and lightnings) are marvellous and not to be understood (
), yet necessary. "For by them He judgeth (chastiseth on the one hand), &c. (and on the other, by them) He giveth meat" (food), &c. (

entries.title: Job 36:32
segments: 32. Rather, "He covereth (both) His hands with light (lightning,
, Margin), and giveth it a command against his adversary" (literally, the one "assailing" Him,
). Thus, as in
, the twofold effects of His waters are set forth, so here, of His light; in the one hand, destructive lightning against the wicked; in the other, the genial light for good to His friends, &c. (
) [UMBREIT].

entries.title: Job 36:33
segments: 33. noise--rather, He revealeth it (literally, "announceth concerning it") to His friend (antithesis to adversary,
, so the Hebrew is translated,
); also to cattle and plants (literally, "that which shooteth up";
). As the genial effect of "water" in the growth of food, is mentioned,

, so here that of "light" in cherishing cattle and plants [UMBREIT]. If English Version, "noise" be retained, translate, "His noise announces concerning Him (His coming in the tempest), the cattle (to announce) concerning Him when He is in the act of rising up" (in the storm). Some animals give various intimations that they are sensible of the approach of a storm [VIRGIL, Georgics, I.373, &c.].
